paper_a.title: Four proofs of the directed Brooks' Theorem

paper_b.title: A short proof of Brooks' theorem

metadata.description: Paper A (Aboulker-Aubian) extends Brooks' theorem to digraphs via the dichromatic number, presenting four distinct proofs (Lovasz greedy, maximal acyclic subdigraph induction, k-tree/Tverberg, and partitioned dicolouring). Paper B (Zajac) gives a single short induction-plus-path proof of the classical undirected Brooks' theorem and extends it to correspondence/signed list-coloring. The pair is an EXT pair: paper A's main result is a directed generalization of paper B's main result, and paper A explicitly cites Brooks 1941 as the undirected origin; some of A's proof techniques echo classical undirected ideas but A's proofs are not direct adaptations of Zajac's specific path-based argument.

matches.explanation: Paper A's definition of $k$-colouring and chromatic number $\chi(G)$ is the standard undirected notion that paper B uses implicitly throughout (paper B never gives an explicit definition node for $k$-colouring; it is taken as given). Marked none because there is no corresponding L1 definition node on the B side.

Acyclic colouring (dicolouring) and dichromatic number $\vec\chi(G)$ is the central directed-graph notion that powers paper A's entire generalization; paper B has no analogue because it works exclusively with undirected proper colouring.
Symmetric digraph $\overleftrightarrow{G}$ is the bridge between undirected and directed colouring ($\chi(G)=\vec\chi(\overleftrightarrow{G})$). Specific to A; B has no need for this construction.
Digon and acyclic digraph definitions are directed-graph specific and have no counterpart in paper B.
$d_{max}$ and $d_{min}$ generalize the undirected $\Delta$ to digraphs via in/out-degrees; paper B uses only undirected $\Delta(G)$, with no in/out distinction.

Symmetric cycles and symmetric complete digraphs are the directed analogues of odd cycles and $K_{k+1}$; paper B uses the underlying undirected exceptions (odd cycle, complete graph) but does not define a corresponding object.

Exception families $\mathcal{B}_k$ collect the directed Brooks exceptions (directed cycles, symmetric odd cycles, symmetric $K_{k+1}$). Paper B's exception set is implicit (odd cycles and $K_{k+1}$); no L1 node carries it explicitly.

Both define a sequential greedy colouring scheme used throughout the proofs. Paper A's directed greedy colouring assigns to $v_i$ a colour avoiding both $N^+\cap\{v_1,\dots,v_{i-1}\}$ and $N^-\cap\{v_1,\dots,v_{i-1}\}$; paper B's PathColor procedure greedily colours all but the last vertex of an uncoloured path. Same role (greedy partial colouring along an order/path) but different formulations: A's is a generic vertex ordering for digraphs, B's is path-restricted with the explicit terminal-uncoloured trick.

$k$-regular digraph and underlying graph $\tilde G$ are directed-specific definitions used in A's proofs to translate to undirected connectivity arguments; B works directly with undirected $k$-regular graphs without needing the underlying-graph construction.

Direct/cyclic compositions, $k$-trees and $k$-leaf/$k$-path are paper-A-specific structural tools for the Tverberg-style proof in Section 4. Paper B has no analogous decomposition; it uses a maximal-path argument instead.

$r$-special digraph, $(r_1,r_2)$-normal partition, and the $\mathcal{P}$-component / acceptable-path / vertex-move machinery are entirely specific to A's partitioned-dicolouring proof (Section 5). Paper B has no analogue.

Both nodes state the classical undirected Brooks theorem (Brooks 1941): a connected graph with $\chi(G)=\Delta(G)+1$ is an odd cycle or complete graph (equivalently, if $\Delta(G)\le k$ and no $K_{k+1}$, then $G$ is $k$-colourable). Paper A cites it as external prior work (origin: external); paper B states it as its main theorem (origin: external, since the citation is to Brooks 1941, but the proof is paper B's contribution). Same mathematical statement up to reformulation (characterization vs. sufficient-condition phrasing).

Paper A's main directed Brooks theorem TP455.2, together with its four variant statements TP455.3 (Lovasz proof), TP455.4 (Rabern-style maximal acyclic subdigraph), TP455.5 (k-tree / Tverberg), and TP455.6 (partitioned dicolouring), all assert the directed analogue $\vec\chi(G)\le\Delta_{max}(G)+1$ with the analogous characterization of the equality cases via $\mathcal{B}_k$. Each is the directed generalization of B's TP419.1 (undirected Brooks). Encoded as a many-to-one cluster correspondence: B has one undirected statement; A repackages the directed extension five times (once as the main theorem, four times once per proof). Confidence high because the EXT relationship is unambiguous and the symmetric-digraph identity $\chi(G)=\vec\chi(\overleftrightarrow G)$ recovers TP419.1 from any of A's directed statements.

Paper A's Lemma lem:reg (LP455.1) states that any connected non-regular digraph satisfies $\vec\chi(G)\le\Delta_{max}(G)$, proved by a BFS-greedy argument from a vertex of small mindegree. Paper B's PSP419.1 is the corresponding reduction step inside the proof: if some vertex of $G$ has degree $<k$, delete it and apply induction (i.e. reduce to the $k$-regular case). They play the same role (eliminate the non-regular case) but with different mechanics (A uses BFS greedy on the full graph; B uses induction by deletion). Cross-level match (L1 lemma vs L2 proof step) justified by the direct functional correspondence; confidence medium because the L2-vs-L1 boundary is somewhat unusual.

Proof of A's lem:reg via BFS ordering is a self-contained proof node; B's analogous step is sub-proof-step rather than a proof node, and is captured implicitly in the LP455.1 <-> PSP419.1 match above.

Both are the proof of the Brooks theorem (directed in A, undirected in B). A's PP455.2 (Lovasz' greedy proof) takes a minimum $k$-regular counterexample and proves four structural claims (2-connectedness, no 2-edge-cut, 2-cuts are stable, two same-side neighbours form a digon or cutset) before contradicting via $G-v$ for an asymmetric arc $uv$. B's PP419.1 takes the same minimum-counterexample / $k$-regular reduction but proceeds by a maximal-path argument (Cases $r=n$ and $r<n$). Same overall framework (minimum $k$-regular counterexample plus a structural contradiction); the structural lemmas differ, so analogous rather than exact. Lovasz' proof is one of A's four; it most closely echoes the standard Lovasz-style undirected argument that B simplifies. The other three of A's proofs (PP455.3, PP455.5, PP455.8) use machinery not present in B and do not have direct B counterparts.
A's Rabern-style proof via a maximal acyclic subdigraph and induction has no analogue in B.
Proof of the $k$-tree trichotomy lemma is internal scaffolding of A's Tverberg-style proof; no analogue in B.
Tverberg-style proof via $k$-tree trichotomy uses A-specific structural decomposition; no analogue in B.
Proof of the special-partition observation belongs to A's partitioned-dicolouring machinery; no analogue in B.
Existence proof for an obstruction-free normal partition, with the four-case $|X|$ analysis (PSP455.1-PSP455.4), is unique to A's partitioned-dicolouring proof.
Partitioned-dicolouring proof of directed Brooks via induction on $\Delta_{max}$ has no analogue in B.

These five claims (2-connectedness of $\tilde G$, no 2-edge-cut, every 2-cut is stable, two same-side neighbours form a digon or cutset, neighbours of $u$ are paired with $v$ in cutsets) are the structural sub-results of A's Lovasz' proof. The classical undirected Lovasz proof uses analogous claims (2-connectedness, no 2-cut, etc.), but B's proof PP419.1 sidesteps them entirely by using the maximal-path argument; B has no L1 claim nodes for these structural facts.
Claims about excluding $\overleftrightarrow K_{k+1}$ and symmetric odd cycles minus arc/digon as induced subdigraphs in the Rabern-style proof (Section 3); no analogue in B.
Claim that the minimum counterexample has no $k$-leaf; internal to A's $k$-tree proof, no B analogue.
Forward and backward directions of the NP-completeness gadget reduction in A's Section 6; no analogue in B.
Observation 4.1 on mindegrees in $k$-trees is paper-A-specific structural observation.
$k$-tree trichotomy lemma is the central structural lemma of A's Tverberg-style proof; no B analogue.
Existence of obstruction-free normal partition is the central lemma of A's partitioned-dicolouring proof (Section 5); no analogue in B.
Special-partition observation supports A's Section 5 partitioned-dicolouring; no analogue in B.
$k$-DICOLOURABILITY problem (cited from Bokal et al.\ 2004) is referenced for A's Section 6 NP-completeness result; no analogue in B.

NP-completeness of $k$-dicolourability restricted to $\Delta_{min}=k$ is a complementary result in A's Section 6 (showing no Brooks analogue holds for $\Delta_{min}$); B contains no complexity-theoretic results.
Gadget-reduction proof for the NP-completeness theorem (with substeps PSP455.5-PSP455.8); no analogue in B.
Remark on greedy bound and Mohar's incomplete proof; aux node, not required to match.

Paper B's Brooks-type theorem for correspondence colouring (and its specialization to signed graphs and list colouring) is paper B's own generalization to a different axis (correspondence/list colouring rather than digraphs). Paper A makes no statement about list/correspondence colouring of digraphs, so this contribution is B-specific within the pair.

List colouring, constraint graph (correspondence colouring), respecting-$F$ colouring, and signed-graph proper colouring are external definitions cited in B's Section 3 to support TP419.2. They have origin: external in B and no analogue in A. Reported as a single composite none entry for compactness.
B's DFS-based linear-time Brooks colouring algorithm derived from the inductive proof has no algorithmic counterpart in A; A's paper is purely structural and gives no algorithm.
